[[File:Brennflaeche-hp-def.svg|thumb|upright=1.3|Focal surfaces (blue, pink) of a hyperbolic [[paraboloid]](white) <math>z=x^2-y^2,\; 0\le x,y\le 0.5</math>]]
[[File:Focal surface.png|thumb|upright=1.3|Focal surfaces (green and red) of a [[monkey saddle]] (blue). At the center point of the monkey saddle the [[Gauss curvature]] is 0, otherwise negative.]] 
For a [[surface (mathematics)|surface]] in three dimension the '''focal surface''', '''surface of centers''' or '''evolute''' is formed by taking the centers of the [[curvature sphere]]s, which are the [[tangent]]ial [[sphere]]s whose radii are the [[Multiplicative inverse|reciprocals]] of one of the [[principal curvature]]s at the point of tangency. Equivalently it is the surface formed by the centers of the circles which [[osculating curve|osculate]] the [[curvature line]]s.<ref>David Hilbert, Stephan Cohn-Vossen: ''Anschauliche Geometrie'', Springer-Verlag, 2011, {{ISBN|3642199488}}, p. 197.</ref><ref>Morris Kline: ''Mathematical Thought From Ancient to Modern Times'', Band 2, Oxford University Press, 1990,{{ISBN|0199840423}}</ref>

[[File:Elliptical umbilic focal surface.png|thumb|right|A surface with an elliptical umbilic, and its focal surface.]]
[[File:Hyperbolic umbilic focal surface.png|thumb|A surface with a hyperbolic umbilic and its focal surface.]]
As the principal curvatures are the eigenvalues of the second fundamental form, there are two at each point, and these give rise to two points of the focal surface on each [[surface normal|normal direction]] to the surface. At points where the [[Gaussian curvature]] is zero, one sheet of the focal surface will have a point at infinity corresponding to the zero principal curvature.

If <math>\vec p</math> is a point of the given surface, <math>\vec n</math> the unit normal and <math>k_1,k_2</math> the [[principal curvature]]s at <math>\vec p</math>, then 
: <math>\vec b_1(\vec p)=\vec p+\frac{\vec n}{k_1} \quad </math> and <math>\quad \vec b_2(\vec p)=\vec p+\frac{\vec n}{k_2}\ </math>
are the corresponding two points of the focal surface.

==Special cases==

#The focal surface of a [[sphere]] consists of a single point, its center. It is the only surface whose focal surface degenerates into a single point.
#The focal surface of a [[Torus]] consists of the directrix circle and the axis of rotation.
#More generally, the focal surface of a [[Dupin cyclide]] consists of a pair of [[focal conics]].<ref>[[Georg Glaeser]], Hellmuth Stachel, Boris Odehnal: ''The Universe of Conics'', Springer, 2016, {{ISBN|3662454505}}, p.&nbsp;147.</ref> The Dupin cyclides are the only surfaces, whose focal surfaces degenerate into two curves.<ref>D. Hilbert, S. Cohn-Vossen:''Geometry and the Imagination'', Chelsea Publishing Company, 1952, p. 218.</ref>
#One part of the focal surface of a [[surface of revolution]] consists of the axis of rotation.
#One part of the focal surface of a [[channel surface]] degenerates to its directrix.
#Two [[confocal quadrics]] (for example an ellipsoid and a hyperboloid of one sheet) can be considered as focal surfaces of a surface.<ref>Hilbert Cohn-Vossen p. 197.</ref>

== Singularities ==
{{See also|Catastrophe theory}}
Away from [[umbilical point]]s, the two points on the two focal surfaces are distinct. At umbilical points, the two sheets come together producing a [[Singularity (mathematics)|singularity]]. There are two types of singularities that are [[Structural stability|structurally stable]]: the elliptical umbilic and the hyperbolic umbilic.

Where the surface has a [[ridge (differential geometry)|ridge]], the focal surface has a [[cuspidal edge]] correspondingly. Generically, through each elliptical umbilic passes three cuspidal edges; through each hyperbolic umbilic passes one cuspidal edge.<ref name="Port">{{Citation |last=Porteous |first=Ian R. |title=Geometric Differentiation |pages=198&ndash;213 |year=2001 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=0-521-00264-8 |authorlink=Ian R. Porteous}}</ref> The parabolic umbilic is not structurally stable.
